clue.text: Like many a claim by Archer, its content is nutty

definitions.text: Like many a claim by Archer
definitions.meaning: first meaning: utter nonsense, as Jeffrey Archer's claims were held to be after his perjury trial
second meaning, read literally: a heap whose contents are testicles, which slang calls nuts

explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Archer, novelist and Tory peer, was jailed for perjury in 2001. Bollocks is British slang for testicles and for rubbish, so 'nutty' content fits the literal heap.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is British slang for complete nonsense, the verdict many passed on the peer's sworn stories.

clue.text: One has to stroke Hattersley's extremities with indifference

parts.note: to pat is to stroke lightly

indicators.note: the extremities of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Someone has to fondle Roy Hattersley's limbs, and does it without enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: Roy Hattersley was Labour's deputy leader in the 1980s.
explanation.definitionFit: Apathy is a lack of interest or concern, the same as indifference.

clue.text: Milo, stiff, tossed (but not to be entered)

indicators.note: tossed like a salad, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: these are the letters to be tossed

explanation.surface: A man called Milo, aroused, pleasures himself, though nobody is to come in.
explanation.definitionFit: A place that is off limits is forbidden territory, somewhere one may not go in.

clue.text: Humiliated and knocked off pedestal?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: lowered in dignity or esteem
second meaning, read whimsically: removed from one's base

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the punning second sense: taken off one's base.
explanation.definitionFit: To debase someone is to degrade or lower them in standing, the same as humiliating them.

clue.text: Fake orgasm about right for an aficionado

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go about the letter for right
an orgasm is a convulsion, so the word before it is thrown into spasms of rearrangement

parts.note: taken as written: the letters that go into spasms

explanation.surface: Faking an orgasm is presented as about right for a devotee.
explanation.walkthrough: Freak means an enthusiast, as in 'health freak' or 'jazz freak'.
explanation.definitionFit: A freak in the sense of 'film freak' is an obsessive fan or devotee of something.

clue.text: To Ernie, heaving on top of Brenda is to try to follow the right course

definitions.text: to try to follow the right course

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece sitting on top of another comes first
heaving tosses these letters about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the letters that are heaved about
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: Ernie, heaving away on top of Brenda, is trying to get it right.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called the Queen Brenda; ER is Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: To orienteer is to navigate a set cross-country route with map and compass, finding each checkpoint in turn.

clue.text: Young bounder on the move in South London

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece placed on another comes first

parts.note: a lamb is a young sheep, famous for skipping and bounding

indicators.note: the following word is on the move, so its letters shift order

parts.note: taken as written: the three letters that are moved

explanation.surface: A young cad is on the go somewhere south of the Thames.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounder' suggests a cad, but here it is an animal that bounds. Lambeth is a borough of south London.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambeth is a London borough on the south bank of the Thames, home to Lambeth Palace.

clue.text: 'He used to be big in politics,' Mary Archer ends in chapter 49

definitions.text: He used to be big in politics

indicators.note: the two final letters go in the middle of the other pieces

parts.note: IL, a loose Roman numeral for forty-nine

indicators.note: the ends of the two names are their final letters

parts.note: the two names whose final letters are taken, from Mary and Archer

explanation.surface: A quotation in chapter 49 of a Mary Archer book about a former political big shot.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Cyril Smith was the very large Liberal MP for Rochdale, so 'big' is literal. Correct Roman for 49 is XLIX.
explanation.definitionFit: Cyril Smith was a famously enormous Liberal MP, a heavyweight in politics in the literal sense.

clue.text: Sad Louis, the first to leave, off for a slash

indicators.note: off means the letters are disturbed, so they are rearranged
the first is the opening letter of the alphabet, told here to leave the word Sad

explanation.surface: A gloomy Louis sees his eldest depart, then nips off to urinate.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a slash is a pee, which is the surface sense; 'the first to leave' takes A out of SAD, then 'off' scrambles SD with LOUIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The oblique stroke used in writing fractions and dates is also called a virgule.

clue.text: Genial Archer's headstrong cock and bull story

parts.note: split as Archer's head plus strong: the head of Archer is its first letter, and strong is F, forte in music
a fable is a made-up tale, just as a cock-and-bull story is

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer, friendly yet stubborn, spins another implausible yarn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Headstrong' reads as one word meaning stubborn; split it, and 'head' takes the first letter while 'strong' gives the musical F.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone genial is friendly and pleasant, which is exactly what an easy-going, approachable person is.

clue.text: "Wicked!" as Mowlam might say, right, to defeated candidate?

parts.note: Mo Mowlam, Labour cabinet minister, might introduce herself with I'm Mo
Al Gore, the losing candidate in the 2000 US presidential election

explanation.surface: Mo Mowlam exclaims 'Wicked!' in youth slang, offering a word of support to a candidate who has lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wicked!' looks like slang approval, but the definition is the plain sense: morally bad.
explanation.definitionFit: Wicked in its plain sense describes evil or sinful conduct, which is what the answer means.

clue.text: (See 22)
In the doghouse, Livingstone rang with tip-off

parts.note: Ken Livingstone, then running for Mayor of London

indicators.note: the tip of the word is taken off, so its opening letter goes

parts.note: a bell that knelled rang out solemnly

explanation.surface: Ken Livingstone, out of favour with his party, phoned someone with a bit of inside information.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tip-off' poses as a piece of inside information; here it asks for the first letter to be removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog sent to its kennel is literally in the doghouse, the idiom for being in disgrace.

clue.text: Might cause a fart to ramble

definitions.meaning: first meaning: gas in the gut, which escapes as a fart
second meaning, said as rhymes with 'find'

explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are spelt alike but said differently: one rhymes with 'tinned', the other with 'find'.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatulence is called wind, and a path that winds meanders or wanders, which is what rambling means.

clue.text: Running costs balls / nuts

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled from one end
nut is slang for the head, so nuts are heads

explanation.surface: An accountant's ledger with a rude aside: the business spends on balls and nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces sound like slang for testicles, but here they are cricket and slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Overheads are a business's ongoing expenses such as rent and power, paid regardless of output.

clue.text: Getting to be newt-like, Ken finally hopes — it's weird

indicators.note: weird letters are odd ones, so they are rearranged into the phrase
finally points to the very end of Ken, its closing letter

parts.note: Ken Livingstone's first name, the source of the closing letter
taken as written into the mix
taken as written into the mix

explanation.surface: Ken Livingstone, who keeps newts, hopes to become more like them, which is odd.
explanation.walkthrough: Ken Livingstone was known for keeping newts. 'Pissed as a newt' is British slang for very drunk, so going out drinking is getting newt-like.
explanation.definitionFit: Out boozing heavily is the way to end up drunk, idiomatically pissed as a newt.

clue.text: Whack much intended, as you might say

indicators.note: spoken aloud the two words run together into one

parts.note: a lot is a great deal, much; meant is intended

explanation.surface: A violent blow that was very much deliberate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whack' looks like a blow, but it is slang for a share, as in 'pay your whack'.
explanation.definitionFit: Whack is British slang for a share or portion, and an allotment is an allocated share.

clue.text: A D.Hirst we rubbished — it's very dull

indicators.note: to rubbish something is to trash it, so these letters are torn up and remade

parts.note: taken as written: the letters that are rubbished

explanation.surface: Critics trashed a Damien Hirst work as tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: Damien Hirst is the British artist known for animals in formaldehyde. 'Dull as dishwater' is the stock phrase behind the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'dull as dishwater' makes the greasy washing-up water a byword for something tedious.

clue.text: Promiscuous English Lib-Dem's married off — he scored successfully

indicators.note: promiscuous means mixed up indiscriminately, so the letters get jumbled
the letter for married is taken off

parts.note: taken as written: Liberal Democrat abbreviated, the letters from which one is dropped

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat who sleeps around dumps his wife and keeps having luck with women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scored' suggests sexual conquest; it means wrote musical scores. Léo Delibes composed the ballets Coppélia and Sylvia.
explanation.definitionFit: Delibes was a French composer whose scores for ballet and opera, such as Lakmé, were great successes.

clue.text: Mass murderer goes to joint in east London

parts.note: Fred West, the Gloucester serial killer
a ham is a joint of meat

explanation.surface: A serial killer heads off to a pub or club in the East End.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a dive or a cannabis spliff; here it is a joint of meat. West Ham is a district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: West Ham is a district of the London Borough of Newham, despite the name in the east of the capital.

clue.text: Archer (unfailingly accurate if you believe the myth) to reveal all?

definitions.text: Archer (unfailingly accurate if you believe the myth)
definitions.meaning: first meaning: William ..., the Swiss legend who shot an apple off his son's head
second meaning: to ... is to disclose, as in ... all

explanation.walkthrough: Every other Archer in this puzzle is Jeffrey; this one is the legendary Swiss bowman.
explanation.definitionFit: William Tell is the mythic Swiss marksman, and to tell is to divulge or let out secrets.

clue.text: "Capital strip, Oliver — getting flipping Rev off!"

indicators.note: the outer letters come off the two words, the tail being Rev turned over, so the answer is the run left inside them

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry at Oliver to get rid of the clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside 'strip, Oliver'; the letters that come off the end, VER, are 'Rev' flipped round, and the leading S goes with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Tripoli is the capital city of Libya.

clue.text: Cancer's a matter of inner resistance

definitions.note: the possessive points to the line of latitude belonging to Cancer, the Tropic of Cancer

indicators.note: the resistance letter goes inside

parts.note: a topic is a matter under discussion

explanation.surface: A medical claim that cancer is down to some internal resistance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cancer' looks like the disease; it is the star sign whose name is given to the northern tropic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tropic of Cancer is the line of latitude about 23 degrees north of the equator.

clue.text: Cull escapee from the slopes?

parts.note: a hill animal that has wandered off and so avoided being culled with the rest of the flock

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes a stray from a hillside flock that evaded slaughter; the phrase is also the biblical image of a wanderer gone astray.
explanation.definitionFit: A stray animal of the flock that went missing on the hills is exactly what the phrase names literally.

clue.text: Like to get up youth in Waldorf, perhaps?

indicators.note: in a down answer getting up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: as means like, in the same way
a lad is a young man

explanation.surface: A young man at the Waldorf hotel wants to rise in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waldorf' suggests the New York hotel; it is the salad of apple, celery and walnuts first served there.
explanation.definitionFit: A Waldorf is a dish of apples, celery and walnuts in mayonnaise, so it is one example.

clue.text: (& 11) Bush-CIA rip-off is the making of Bush

indicators.note: the word before has gone off, rearranging its letters

parts.note: taken as written: the letters that are ripped and rearranged

explanation.surface: A CIA swindle involving George W. Bush is what made him president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' looks like the American president; the second Bush is slang for pubic hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A bush in slang is a thick growth of pubic hair, so its individual strands are what it is made of.

clue.text: What to do with a stiff one in wintertime

definitions.text: What to do with a stiff one

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the longer word that follows

parts.note: the word whose middle holds the answer, after its opening W

explanation.surface: A drinker's tip: what to do with a strong drink on a cold winter night.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'stiff one' suggests a strong drink; here it is a stiff, slang for a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury, which is what one does with a dead body.

clue.text: Soho liberal's head turned when hugged by sexually unfussy Russian bounders

indicators.note: the jumbled letters are held inside the outer pair

parts.note: bi, short for bisexual, attracted to either sex

indicators.note: the letters of Soho plus one more are turned about into a new order

parts.note: taken as written: the London district's name, to be turned about

indicators.note: the head of liberal is its first letter

parts.note: the word whose head, its first letter, is taken

explanation.surface: A Soho liberal is cuddled by a crowd of uninhibited Russian cads.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounders' looks like cads; here it means leapers, the dancers of the Moscow ballet company.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bolshoi Ballet is Moscow's great dance company, whose dancers leap about the stage.

clue.text: Drip in local, back for piss-taking session

indicators.note: the dripping word goes inside the other
the word for the drinking house is read back to front

parts.note: a local is a British drinker's nearby pub
to drip is to ooze out slowly

explanation.surface: A wet weakling in the pub returns for a session of being mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piss-taking' suggests mockery; here it is literal, a session of taking piss as in drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A booze-up is a heavy drinking session; 'piss' is British slang for alcohol, so taking it means drinking.

clue.text: The reverse of M&S? Perhaps not what its shareholders think

definitions.meaning: M&S reversed is S&M, sadism and masochism

definitions.text: Perhaps not what its shareholders think
definitions.meaning: a joke that investors in Marks & Spencer would hardly call the store kinky

explanation.walkthrough: M&S is Marks & Spencer, the staid British high-street chain; flip the letters and you get the kinky abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: S&M is the common shorthand for sadomasochism, deriving pleasure from inflicting or receiving pain.
